name: Iowa Army Ammunition Plant
known_energetics: Bulk lead azide stored wetted in 68 55-gallon plastic drums in two earth-covered magazines; Col. Aaron C. Teller (71st Ordnance Group EOD) states the total weight is 9,773.5 lb. The plant also has a conventional munitions load-assemble-pack mission. This draft does not inventory other energetics on site.
notable_incidents: 2026-11: Army plan to destroy 68 drums of crystallized, unserviceable lead azide by controlled in-place detonation in two earth-covered magazines. EPA issued an emergency RCRA permit on Nov 13, 2026. The shot did not take place on Nov 20 or Nov 23, 2026, and remained subject to a court stay and a reported presidential stand-down order.
current_status: As of Nov 23, 2026 (America/Phoenix): the planned in-place detonation had not occurred. The original date was Nov 20; the Army postponed to Nov 23, then announced Nov 25. The Eighth Circuit issued an administrative stay of EPA's emergency treatment permit on Nov 19, pending a ruling on the emergency stay motion in No. 26-3374; as of a CourtListener docket review on Nov 23, that merits ruling had not issued. Iowa Public Radio reported that President Trump posted on Truth Social on Nov 23 that he ordered the military not to proceed until the Eighth Circuit agrees they can go forward, and subject to Gov.-elect Rob Sand agreeing. IAAAP also holds a regular RCRA OB/OD permit (EPA ID IA7213820445) listed as permitted through Sept 28, 2028. The emergency permit for in-place magazine detonation is a separate authorization, issued Nov 13, 2026, effective through Feb 11, 2027.
notes: The closest documented historical analog for bulk lead azide in deteriorating 55-gallon drums is Savanna Army Depot (1984). A March 21, 2014 Army article attributed DoD's 2004 green-primaries work to concern over a 40-year-old deteriorating lead azide stockpile at IAAAP. A separate research log kept with this draft has the claim-by-claim review.

known_energetics: William Shaneyfelt, safety officer at Savanna Army Depot Activity, described Vietnam-era surplus bulk lead azide in deteriorating 55-gallon drums in a 1984 paper to the DoD Explosives Safety Board. Electrolysis destroyed about half the stockpile; the remainder was repacked. The public record reviewed for this draft does not establish what happened to the remaining drums after 1984.
notable_incidents: 1984: Shaneyfelt paper (21st Explosives Safety Seminar, Houston, Aug 28–30, 1984): surplus bulk lead azide in deteriorating drums; sale attempts failed; electrolytic destruction halted after about half the stockpile; remaining leaking drums were repacked. The paper also describes a process-building contamination accident in which sodium azide washdown reacted with brass/copper debris and caused a 'loud, though not extremely dangerous, explosion.' That event was not a storage-drum detonation.

current_status: A former Army depot. EPA FRS lists BRAC and SEMS interests under ID IL3210020803. It is not on EPA's current OB/OD operating list. Present land use and whether any energetic material remains were not independently confirmed in this draft.

coordinate_method: INTERPOLATION-MAP; accuracy_value=30; reference: point where substance is released
known_energetics: M6 propellant and clean-burning igniter (CBI) left from Explo Systems contractor storage of Army-origin material. EPA approved contained-burn destruction of about 16 million pounds of M6 and CBI in June 2016. These are HD 1.3 propellant/igniter materials, not primary explosives such as lead azide.
notable_incidents: 2012-10-15: Explosion of a magazine at Explo Systems, Camp Minden. EPA chronology: Louisiana State Police later identified about 10 million pounds of unsecured M6; the town of Doyline (about 400 homes) was evacuated during operational hours. | 2013-06: Army Explosives Safety Board report cited in the EPA chronology: the probability of an explosives event related to long-term storage of M6 at Camp Minden was 'likely'; the Board recommended open burn/open detonation within two years. | 2016-06-13: EPA approved a contained-burn system after tests showed 99.99% destruction of chemicals of concern, for about 16 million pounds of M6 and CBI. | 2016-09-29: About 120,960 pounds of CBI auto-ignited in an earth-covered magazine and destroyed the bunker. Louisiana National Guard reported no injuries. An Army Explosive Safety Technical Assistance Visit then advised that remaining CBI was too dangerous to handle and should be destroyed in place, with some magazines remotely ignited because entering them was not acceptable.
permit_status: Not on EPA's current OB/OD operating list
current_status: The 2012–2016 emergency disposal campaign used a contained-burn chamber after open burning was dropped following public opposition. This draft has not independently confirmed current residual holdings, if any, after that campaign.
notes: Closest recent official parallel to IAAAP's 'cannot safely move it, destroy in place' finding, though the chemistry differs.
